tei:titleStmt.tei:title: אֵימָתַי נִגְלָה לַנֶּאֱהָב
Eimatai Niglah la-Ne'ehav — an original 'Aqedah piyyuṭ by Isaac Gantwerk Mayer

tei:div.tei:head: Eimatai Niglah la-Ne'ehav — an original 'Aqedah piyyuṭ by Isaac Gantwerk Mayer

tei:lg.tei:l: When was it revealed to the beloved,
the only son, as precious as gold,
weaned in a feast of love,
“Your path is to go up in flame?”
Did you know in the land of Philistia,
when he woke up early in the renewed sun —
your elder, first of three,
dreamed a dream to do a shameful commandment?
You walked with him three days;
you knew there was no lamb for the coals.
As you asked, “Where is the unblemished lamb?”
to understand if your destination was bloodshed.
When did you understand his answer?
Understand, the son is the very lamb!
He arranged the wood of his fire;
a time came, doubtlessly you knew it.
The sages interpreted that you accepted:
command to command, rule to rule, you did not panic.
You called to the one from whom you were raised,
“It is only my merit that I be tied up.
Keep my slaughter as per the law!
Bring to my mother Yiscah
my ashes, worthy of the chamber;
please do not delay, go forth!”
You knew, according to the midrashim,
your destination was to go up in flame.
I must bring a new novelty:
this wisdom is not in the written Pentateuch!
A sacrifice, though you did not pass on,
you were, as if you were burned.
Is it not said that you did not speak to him?
Between Abraham and you, you were scattered!
It is a law for your seed, bearing
the memory of the slaughterer and the lamb.
Bring near our song, like ascending smoke,
to the Sovereign Deity sitting on the throne!

tei:note.tei:p: Isaac. Most of this poem is addressing Isaac directly.
Abraham. For most of this poem, the second person is Isaac, and the third person is Abraham.

According to the Rambam, Guide III 24:10, Abraham’s commandment to slaughter his son was received in a dream. Later commentators emphasized the fact that Abraham woke up early in the morning to do it.
According to the midrash, Sarah. See Sifrei Bamidbar 99:1 and Megillah 14a.
Referring, by synecdoche, to the Temple
Nowhere in the written Torah does it state that Isaac knew what was happening.
After the Akedah, Abraham and Isaac are never in the same location again. The next time Isaac sees his father it is his corpse. There is total separation between the two.
A formulaic conclusion for an ‘aqedah poem, designed to lead into a recitation of the Thirteen Attributes.
